title: Data races, Atomic and Mutex
body: When two domains touch the same mutable location and at least one writes, you have a data race. OCaml 5 has a memory model that keeps races from corrupting memory, but the result is still wrong: `n := !n + 1` is a read, an add and a write, so two domains can both read 5 and both write 6, and one increment is lost.

`Atomic.t` makes single operations indivisible. `Atomic.incr`, `Atomic.fetch_and_add` and `Atomic.compare_and_set` are executed without interruption, so a shared counter built from them never loses an update. Writing `Atomic.set c (Atomic.get c + 1)` is *not* atomic overall, because another domain can run between the get and the set.

For updates that involve several fields or a data structure, use a lock: `Mutex.protect m (fun () -> ...)` runs the function with the mutex held and releases it even on an exception. Prefer atomics for one counter or flag, and a mutex around code that must see a consistent whole.
challenge: The starter Counter wraps a plain `int ref`, so the test (4 domains each incrementing 200,000 times) loses updates. Reimplement `create`, `incr` and `get` on top of `Atomic` so the total is exactly 800,000.
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .` on the starter to watch the assertion fail because of lost updates, then fix src/counter.ml. Edit only that file.
question: Why is `Atomic.set c (Atomic.get c + 1)` still racy?
correct: The get and the set are two separate atomic steps, so another domain can update the counter in between
wrong: Atomic.set is not allowed after Atomic.get
Atomic values can only be read
reasoning: Atomicity applies to each operation individually; a read-modify-write needs one operation such as fetch_and_add or a compare_and_set loop.

mutations.replace: let incr c = Atomic.set c (Atomic.get c + 1)
